Four-legion consular norm plus allied alae; metal armor still socially graded.
First Punic War mobilization; mail adoption beginning among wealthier infantry.

Twenty-five citizen legions in service near the wartime peak, expanded with allied formations; strength per unit is uncertain.
Postwar drawdown but sustained overseas commitments; mail increasingly common.
Lower peacetime establishment after the Macedonian wars.
Late Republican armies; mail is standard for legionary heavy infantry.
Civil-war peak across competing Roman armies; the central estimate converts roughly sixty nominal legions and associated troops to personnel.
Augustan settlement and demobilization toward twenty-eight permanent legions plus auxiliaries and other forces.

Flavian standing army after civil war, including auxiliaries.
Trajanic maximum; roughly thirty legions plus auxiliaries, fleets, and specialist formations.

Severan expansion to thirty-three legions; published totals vary from about 380,000 to roughly 500,000 depending on included forces.
Late third-century reconstruction; paper strength, effective strength, and unit definitions diverge.
Diocletianic establishment; larger totals partly reflect more numerous smaller units.
Combined field and frontier forces across the empire; high uncertainty.
Combined eastern and western establishments at the administrative division.
